title: Black smokers on the seabed gush water above 400 °C that the pressure keeps from boiling
body: On mid-ocean ridges and undersea volcanoes, seawater seeps down through cracks, is heated by hot rock above magma, and comes back out loaded with dissolved metals at temperatures that can top **400 °C**. It doesn’t boil, because the weight of the ocean above raises the boiling point, so the water stays liquid or becomes a supercritical fluid. When it hits the surrounding water, at about 2 °C, the metals drop out as dark sulfide minerals: that is the black “smoke”, and it slowly builds the chimney.

cover.alt: A pale mineral chimney on the dark seafloor with a cloud of black smoky water billowing from its side

slides.alt: Deep-sea footage lit by a submersible’s lights: black, smoke-like water billows out of a tall, pale mineral chimney, then the view moves to a cluster of spiky chimneys on the seafloor.
slides.caption: A vent puffing black ‘smoke’, filmed in 2016 on NOAA’s Deepwater Exploration of the Marianas expedition in the western Pacific.
slides.credit: NOAA Ocean Exploration · Public domain · excerpt

slides.label: the fastest chimney growth on record
slides.text: Chimneys can reach 60 m. One off Oregon, nicknamed Godzilla, grew to 40 m before it fell over in 1996.

slides.question: What makes the smoke of a black smoker black?
slides.explanation: Dissolved metals in the hot vent fluid drop out as dark sulfide minerals when it meets the near-freezing seawater.
